newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's campaign trail awash with cash.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's campaign trail awash with cash.

text.p: Key Mexican elections next month come with a difference: for the first time, millions of dollars in public funding mean opposition parties can mount an effective media challenge to the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

Two weeks before national congressional elections on July 6, slick television advertising campaigns and radio spots are giving main opposition parties a public profile that used to be the exclusive preserve of the PRI.

Total government funding in the races for the Chamber of Deputies, a quarter of the Senate and Mexico City's mayor plus additional resources for routine party activities mean a staggering $300 million is available -- five times the amount spent in the 1994 presidential election.

"The generosity with which the state gave funds to the parties has already had a major impact on their campaigns," Jorge Alcocer, head of a respected political magazine Voz y Voto (Voice and Vote), told Reuters.
"It is the first federal campaign in Mexico ever to be carried out mainly on radio and television. Never before in Mexico's electoral history have we had such an extensive opposition presence there."

Ironically, the generous government cash is the result of a reform both main opposition parties opposed when it came to Congress last year. The conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) charged that the funding was excessive in a country where half the population survive on less than $7 a day.

But the PRI, which gets the lion's share of the cash thanks to a formula based on previous election results, rammed through the law. Government officials said they wanted to encourage democracy and keep money from illicit sources such as the flourishing drug trade from finding its way into campaign coffers, as happened in Colombia.

For specific campaign activity, the PRI $112 million, the PAN $66 million and the PRD $49 million. Partly thanks to the public funding, polls show that for the first time opposition parties are presenting a serious threat to the PRI majority in the lower house of Congress.
The PRI, with 68 years in power, still has by far the deepest pockets and it can outspend opponents on almost every campaign stump and media network nationwide, analysts say.

"However, you also have to look at the efficiency of parties in using their money," political analyst Miguel Angel Granados Chapa said. "The PRI is so used to having a lot of money that it doesn't use it very well."

He said the PRD, once the favourite of long-haired leftist intellectuals, perhaps best reflects the face-lift a dose of hard cash can buy. Its breezy and costly television spots of a rising Aztec sun ending the long night of PRI rule reach out to housewives, students and workers with catchy familiarity.

In the first-ever race for mayor of Mexico City, PRD candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas has, his aides say, twice as much to spend this election as he was given in public funds for his failed bid for the presidency in 1994. He is easily the front-runner in the capital and his messages on national television have proved so popular pollsters say he has lifted the PRD vote across the country.
In the offices of the PAN and the PRD, campaign workers say they still work under tight budget constraints and both parties have rejected some of the public funds made available.

"For a country like ours with such a terrible economic crisis, it is almost offensive that political parties have so much money," Octavio Romero, finance director of the PRD, said. "Money is the mother of the devil."

The only party apparently unashamed of its riches is the PRI, which for decades used whatever means was at its disposal, even blatant fraud, to maintain its grip on power. PRI deputies spoke out in favour of even higher levels of public funding when the law was debated last year.

Silver-service campaign dinners dotted with media personalities are still regular PRI fare, and at its political rallies around the country impoverished Mexicans are often wooed by free food, T-shirts and handouts of medicines.
